children.text: A metallic ring of radius R carries uniform charge q. Its circular toroidal cross-section has radius a≪R, neglected except in part D. Its plane is xy and its axis is z. Potential is zero at infinity. An electron has mass m and charge −e, e>0, and does not perturb the ring charge distribution. Near the origin use \((1+x)^s\simeq1+sx+s(s-1)x^2/2\). In lens operation the electron speed v along z is approximately constant, with kinetic energy E=mv²/2. The ring is activated only while the electron packet crosses \(|z|<d/2\), where d≪R. Work in the paraxial limit r≪R, with focal distances much greater than d, ignoring magnetic fields and propagation delay. Parts D and E replace instantaneous charging by a capacitance C and contact resistance R0. For focusing choose the appropriate signed supply V0.

statement.text:
Electrostatic lens
A metallic ring of radius R carries uniform charge q. Its circular toroidal cross-section has radius a≪R, neglected except in part D. Its plane is xy and its axis is z. Potential is zero at infinity. An electron has mass m and charge −e, e>0, and does not perturb the ring charge distribution. Near the origin use \((1+x)^s\simeq1+sx+s(s-1)x^2/2\). In lens operation the electron speed v along z is approximately constant, with kinetic energy E=mv²/2. The ring is activated only while the electron packet crosses \(|z|<d/2\), where d≪R. Work in the paraxial limit r≪R, with focal distances much greater than d, ignoring magnetic fields and propagation delay. Parts D and E replace instantaneous charging by a capacitance C and contact resistance R0. For focusing choose the appropriate signed supply V0.

a.1. Axial potential
Find Φ(z) on the axis.
a.2. Near-centre axial expansion
Expand through the first position-dependent nonzero term for |z|≪R.
a.3. Axial electron force
Find the leading signed axial force and the sign of q needed for oscillations.
a.4. Axial oscillation frequency
For the stable sign of q find ω.
b.1. Radial potential coefficient
In the ring plane let Φ(r)≈q(α+βr²). Derive β.
b.2. Radial electron force
Find the leading radial force and the sign of q for radial harmonic confinement.
c.1. Pulsed lens focal length

With instantaneous switching, find f in terms of β and the given quantities. Initially the electron packet is parallel to z.
c.2. Finite-source image
A point source is on the axis distance b>f from the ring and emits at small angles. Find image distance c.
c.3. Thin-lens relation
Calculate 1/b+1/c and determine whether the optical thin-lens relation holds.
d.1. Thin torus capacitance
Retain cross-section radius a≪R and calculate C to leading thin-ring accuracy.
d.2. Charging waveform

At entry connect the ring through R0 to V0, and at exit connect it through R0 to ground. Time t=0 is passage through the ring plane. Find and sketch q(t), and give its maximum signed charge q0.
e.1. Focal length with finite charging
Assume f/v≫R0C and d/v is comparable to R0C. Find f, including the discharge tail after the electron exits the nominal active region.
e.2. Effective charge
Express qeff such that the result has the instantaneous-lens form with q replaced by qeff.

children.text: Every ring element is the same distance \(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\) away, so \[\Phi(z)=\frac q{4\pi\epsilon_0\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}.\]
Because electron potential energy is −eΦ, \(F_z=e\partial_z\Phi=-eqz/(4\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). It restores toward the centre for q>0.
Compare \(m\ddot z=-m\omega^2z\) with A3: \(\omega=\sqrt{eq/(4\pi\epsilon_0mR^3)}\), with q>0.

Expand \((R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\phi)^{-1/2}\) and average cosφ and cos²φ around the ring. The result is \(\Phi(r)=q[1+r^2/(4R^2)]/(4\pi\epsilon_0R)\). Thus \(\beta=1/(16\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). This also follows from the charge-free Laplace equation and the axial expansion.
\(F_r=e\partial_r\Phi=2eq\beta r=eqr/(8\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). Radial restoration requires q<0, opposite to axial restoration. The ring cannot provide simultaneous static confinement in all directions.
The active time is d/v. Radial impulse gives \(\Delta v_r=2eq\beta rd/(mv)\), negative for q<0. The subsequent crossing time is −r/Δvr. Thus \[f=-\frac{mv^2}{2eq\beta d}=-\frac E{eq\beta d}.\]

At the ring the initial radial velocity is vr/b. Add the impulse from C1, then propagate to the axis: \[c=-\left(\frac1b+\frac{eq\beta d}{E}\right)^{-1}.\] With b>f and q<0 the denominator is negative and c>0.
C2 gives \(1/b+1/c=-eq\beta d/E=1/f\). Thus the same thin-lens equation holds in the stated impulse approximation.

Split the ring at a small angular cutoff η with a/R≪η≪1. The nearby piece is approximately a straight line and contributes \(q\ln(2\eta R/a)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The remainder contributes \(q\ln(4/\eta)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The arbitrary cutoff cancels, giving \[C=\frac{4\pi^2\epsilon_0R}{\ln(8R/a)}.\]

Write τ=R0C and t0=d/v. The continuous waveform is \[q(t)=\begin{cases}0&t<-t_0/2,\\CV_0[1-e^{-(t+t_0/2)/\tau}]&-t_0/2\le t\le t_0/2,\\CV_0(1-e^{-t_0/\tau})e^{-(t-t_0/2)/\tau}&t>t_0/2.\end{cases}\] The largest magnitude occurs at exit, with \(q_0=CV_0(1-e^{-d/(vR_0C)})\). For focusing V0<0, so the curve dips below zero and returns exponentially to it.
e.1. Focal length with finite charging

During the impulse r changes negligibly and the electron remains near the ring because vR0C is of order d≪R. Integrating \(R_0\dot q+q/C=V(t)\) over the full charging and discharge history gives \(\int qdt=CV_0d/v\), independent of R0. Therefore \(\Delta v_r=(2e\beta r/m)CV_0d/v\) and \[f=-\frac E{e\beta CV_0d}.\] Omitting the discharge tail would give a different and incomplete impulse.
The complete charge-time integral matches a rectangular pulse of height \(q_{eff}=CV_0\) and duration d/v. It is not the peak charge q0.

solution.text:
Electrostatic lens
a.1. Axial potential
Every ring element is the same distance \(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\) away, so \[\Phi(z)=\frac q{4\pi\epsilon_0\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}.\]
a.2. Near-centre axial expansion
Binomial expansion gives \[\Phi(z)\simeq\frac q{4\pi\epsilon_0R}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{2R^2}\right).\]
a.3. Axial electron force
Because electron potential energy is −eΦ, \(F_z=e\partial_z\Phi=-eqz/(4\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). It restores toward the centre for q>0.
a.4. Axial oscillation frequency
Compare \(m\ddot z=-m\omega^2z\) with A3: \(\omega=\sqrt{eq/(4\pi\epsilon_0mR^3)}\), with q>0.
b.1. Radial potential coefficient
Expand \((R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\phi)^{-1/2}\) and average cosφ and cos²φ around the ring. The result is \(\Phi(r)=q[1+r^2/(4R^2)]/(4\pi\epsilon_0R)\). Thus \(\beta=1/(16\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). This also follows from the charge-free Laplace equation and the axial expansion.
b.2. Radial electron force
\(F_r=e\partial_r\Phi=2eq\beta r=eqr/(8\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). Radial restoration requires q<0, opposite to axial restoration. The ring cannot provide simultaneous static confinement in all directions.
c.1. Pulsed lens focal length
The active time is d/v. Radial impulse gives \(\Delta v_r=2eq\beta rd/(mv)\), negative for q<0. The subsequent crossing time is −r/Δvr. Thus \[f=-\frac{mv^2}{2eq\beta d}=-\frac E{eq\beta d}.\]
c.2. Finite-source image
At the ring the initial radial velocity is vr/b. Add the impulse from C1, then propagate to the axis: \[c=-\left(\frac1b+\frac{eq\beta d}{E}\right)^{-1}.\] With b>f and q<0 the denominator is negative and c>0.
c.3. Thin-lens relation
C2 gives \(1/b+1/c=-eq\beta d/E=1/f\). Thus the same thin-lens equation holds in the stated impulse approximation.
d.1. Thin torus capacitance
Split the ring at a small angular cutoff η with a/R≪η≪1. The nearby piece is approximately a straight line and contributes \(q\ln(2\eta R/a)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The remainder contributes \(q\ln(4/\eta)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The arbitrary cutoff cancels, giving \[C=\frac{4\pi^2\epsilon_0R}{\ln(8R/a)}.\]
d.2. Charging waveform
Write τ=R0C and t0=d/v. The continuous waveform is \[q(t)=\begin{cases}0&t<-t_0/2,\\CV_0[1-e^{-(t+t_0/2)/\tau}]&-t_0/2\le t\le t_0/2,\\CV_0(1-e^{-t_0/\tau})e^{-(t-t_0/2)/\tau}&t>t_0/2.\end{cases}\] The largest magnitude occurs at exit, with \(q_0=CV_0(1-e^{-d/(vR_0C)})\). For focusing V0<0, so the curve dips below zero and returns exponentially to it.
e.1. Focal length with finite charging
During the impulse r changes negligibly and the electron remains near the ring because vR0C is of order d≪R. Integrating \(R_0\dot q+q/C=V(t)\) over the full charging and discharge history gives \(\int qdt=CV_0d/v\), independent of R0. Therefore \(\Delta v_r=(2e\beta r/m)CV_0d/v\) and \[f=-\frac E{e\beta CV_0d}.\] Omitting the discharge tail would give a different and incomplete impulse.
e.2. Effective charge
The complete charge-time integral matches a rectangular pulse of height \(q_{eff}=CV_0\) and duration d/v. It is not the peak charge q0.
